doc.title: Frank Tate interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001

title: Bill Charlap and how young players develop
summary: Tate admires Charlap and Harry Allen and compares to Rowles and Clark Terry.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: The future’s in some good hands there.

Oh boy. He’s got a record out, he did “The Man that Got Away.” Ruby plays that too so I’m hoping we’ll play it. It’s [scats] it’s as slow as you can get and swings so hard and he’s just a real force to be reckoned with in this business. You know and I’m listening to him and he’s in his I guess his early, mid-‘30s, I don’t know what his age is. But I was listening to a Jimmy Rowles record from the ‘50s the other day when Jimmy would have been about the age that Bill Charlap is now. And you listen to Bill Charlap and you think well there’s no way he can improve on what he’s doing. But he probably will. Listen to what Jimmy Rowles — listen to Clark Terry from the ‘50s and listen to the latter day Clark Terry and how his style and everything about him at some point in the ‘60s or whenever it was took a quantum leap forward in all respects. He was always a great player but he got considerably greater. And Jimmy Rowles did the same thing. And so I listen to guys like Harry Allen and Bill Charlap and I say there’s no way they can improve on what they’re doing right now but who knows. I hope I stick around long enough to see what they both do. Harry is another one. He’s just a phenom. So.
I really do like listening to him.
